title: Grade 5 Science — Fri, Jun 20
description: Respiratory System — Day 5 of 5: Mixed review — full system, lung health
subject: science

questions.question: The correct order of air flow into the body is:
questions.explanation: Air flows: Nose → Pharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli.

questions.question: Gas exchange occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Gas exchange (O₂ in, CO₂ out of blood) happens at the alveoli — tiny air sacs with thin walls and rich blood supply.

questions.question: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contracts → moves down → chest expands → pressure drops → air flows in.

questions.question: O₂ is carried in blood by:
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin (in red blood cells) binds O₂ in the lungs and releases it at body cells.

questions.question: CO₂ moves from blood into alveoli because:
options: CO₂ concentration is higher in blood than in alveolar air — diffusion
questions.explanation: Diffusion: CO₂ is at HIGH concentration in blood → moves to LOW concentration in alveolar air → exhaled.

questions.question: The trachea is kept open by:
questions.explanation: C-shaped cartilage rings surround the trachea to keep it open (so it doesn't collapse when you breathe in). The open part faces the oesophagus.

questions.question: Which organ separates the chest cavity from the abdomen and drives breathing?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is the muscular floor of the chest cavity. Its contractions and relaxations are the primary driver of breathing.

questions.question: A person with asthma has narrowed airways during an attack. This makes breathing:
options: Harder — less air can flow in and out; breathing becomes wheezy and difficult
questions.explanation: Asthma narrows the airways (bronchospasm + mucus), increasing resistance. Less air can pass → breathing is laboured and wheezy.

questions.question: Pneumonia is an infection of the:
options: Lungs — alveoli fill with fluid/pus, reducing gas exchange
questions.explanation: Pneumonia infects the lungs. Alveoli fill with fluid or pus, blocking gas exchange. Symptoms: fever, cough, difficulty breathing.

questions.question: Coughing is a protective reflex that:
options: Forcefully expels irritants, mucus, or foreign particles from the airways
questions.explanation: Coughing is the body's mechanism to clear the airway of mucus, dust, pathogens, or foreign objects. It is a defensive reflex.

questions.question: How does exercise benefit the respiratory system long term?
options: It damages the lungs from overuse
It strengthens respiratory muscles and increases lung capacity
questions.explanation: Regular exercise strengthens the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, increases lung capacity, and makes the respiratory system more efficient.

questions.question: Air pollution harms the respiratory system by:
options: Irritating and damaging the airways, triggering asthma, and causing cancer
questions.explanation: Air pollution (particulates, NO₂, SO₂, ozone) irritates airways, triggers asthma, reduces lung function, and can cause lung cancer with long-term exposure.

questions.question: The nose, trachea, and bronchi are lined with:
options: Cilia and mucus that trap and sweep out dust and pathogens
questions.explanation: The airways are lined with cilia (tiny hair-like projections) and mucus. Dust and pathogens stick to mucus; cilia sweep the mucus upward to be swallowed or expelled.

questions.question: Trees and forests help human respiration by:
options: Absorbing CO₂ and releasing oxygen through photosynthesis
Creating more water vapour in air
questions.explanation: Trees absorb CO₂ (which we exhale) and release O₂ (which we inhale) through photosynthesis. Deforestation reduces O₂ supply and increases CO₂ in the atmosphere.

questions.question: WEEK STAR: A student runs a 400 m race. Describe the changes in the respiratory system during and after the race.
options: Breathing rate increases (more O₂ needed, more CO₂ produced); diaphragm and rib muscles work faster; after race, breathing gradually slows back to normal
Breathing rate stays the same throughout
Breathing rate slows during exercise to conserve energy
questions.explanation: During: muscles need more O₂ → breathing rate increases (40–60 breaths/min); diaphragm works faster. More CO₂ triggers faster breathing. After: CO₂ normalises, breathing slows. This is the normal respiratory response to exercise.
